question: What is the primary goal of a Just Culture in healthcare?

options.A: Protecting negligent healthcare workers from any legal action
options.B: Ensuring every medical mistake receives an immediate suspension
options.C: Encouraging safe reporting of errors without unfair punishment
options.D: Eliminating all human errors completely from hospital wards

explanation: A Just Culture prioritizes transparent reporting so systemic issues can be fixed without driving staff to hide mistakes out of fear. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h1)

question: Why does a punitive blame culture put future patients at risk?

options.A: Management increases the cost of healthcare services for patients
options.B: Doctors refuse to work with nurses who make medication mistakes
options.C: Staff hide errors instead of reporting them, keeping system flaws hidden
options.D: Nurses become too confident and stop following hospital protocols

explanation: When healthcare workers fear harsh punishment, they conceal near misses and mistakes, preventing the hospital from fixing underlying system hazards. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h1)

question: What happens in a traditional blame culture when a medication error occurs?

options.A: The hospital investigates underlying equipment failures
options.B: The individual involved faces immediate punishment
options.C: Management updates safety policies for all nursing units

explanation: A blame culture focuses entirely on finding a person to punish rather than examining the root causes of the mistake. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h2)

question: What is a major limitation of a strict no-blame culture?

options.A: It forces nurses to hide all minor clinical mistakes
options.B: It completely stops the reporting of near-miss incidents
options.C: It increases the frequency of punitive disciplinary hearings
options.D: It fails to address reckless or blatantly careless behavior

explanation: A zero-accountability approach can excuse dangerous, reckless actions that put patients in harm's way, which compromises overall safety. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h2)

question: Which scenario best represents a failure of system accountability?

options.A: Two different medications have identical packaging stored side by side
options.B: An auxiliary staff member ignores a ringing patient monitor
options.C: A nurse deliberately skips checking a patient identity band
options.D: A clinician refuses to document vital signs during an emergency

explanation: Poor packaging design and flawed drug storage are systemic hazards created by the organization, not the individual nurse. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h3)

question: What does individual accountability require from a registered nurse in clinical practice?

options.A: Covering up minor near-misses to protect the hospital image
options.B: Purchasing modern medical equipment for underfunded wards
options.C: Following established safety standards and exercising sound judgment
options.D: Accepting blame for all equipment failures in the hospital

explanation: Nurses are individually accountable for performing their duties professionally and adhering to safety protocols within their control. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h3)

question: How should nursing management handle an honest human error made by a competent nurse?

options.A: Demote the nurse to a junior auxiliary staff position
options.B: Suspend the nurse immediately without a formal hearing
options.C: Issue a stern written warning placed in the personnel file
options.D: Console the staff member and evaluate the system design

explanation: Human errors are inadvertent slips, so punishing the nurse does nothing to prevent future occurrences; fixing the system does. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h4)

question: Which action by a healthcare worker is classified as reckless behavior?

options.A: Forgetting to document a routine dose of oral paracetamol
options.B: Taking a familiar shortcut during a busy morning ward round
options.C: Reporting to clinical duty while under the influence of alcohol
options.D: Misreading a confusing drug label on a high-alert medication

explanation: Reckless behavior involves a conscious, intentional disregard of obvious, substantial risks to patient safety. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of using the substitution test in nursing management?

options.A: To determine if peers would likely make the same choice in that situation
options.B: To test the clinical competency of newly graduated nursing interns
options.C: To measure the exact financial cost of a medication administration error
options.D: To substitute a suspended nurse with temporary agency staff members

explanation: The substitution test checks if the environment and pressure drove the mistake, helping managers see if any peer would have done the same. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h5)

question: A manager asks if another nurse under identical conditions would make the same mistake. What tool is being applied?
explanation: The substitution test specifically evaluates whether the action was an isolated individual lapse or a systemic response to pressure. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h5)

question: What does psychological safety mean for clinical nursing staff?

options.A: Working night shifts without any supervision from senior doctors
options.B: Assuming zero responsibility for any medication mistakes made
options.C: Feeling safe to speak up about errors without fear of unfair punishment
options.D: Ignoring hospital protocols during emergency trauma resuscitations

explanation: Psychological safety ensures workers can report mistakes and voice concerns openly without fearing retribution. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h6)

question: How should nurse leaders respond when staff members submit an incident report?

options.A: By penalizing the entire ward shift for poor supervision
options.B: With immediate disciplinary suspension for the reporter
options.C: By keeping the report strictly confidential from the team
options.D: With curiosity to investigate systemic workflow issues

explanation: Viewing reports with curiosity encourages continued transparency and helps leadership uncover and fix hidden hazards. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h6)

question: Why do traditional warnings fail to stop errors in under-resourced Nigerian hospital settings?

options.A: Patients prefer traditional remedies over orthodox medical care
options.B: Training institutions do not teach basic pharmacology principles
options.C: Nurses do not respect hospital management or disciplinary committees
options.D: Systemic challenges like power outages and shortages drive at-risk behaviors

explanation: When systemic resource deficits force staff into daily shortcuts, punishing individuals does not solve the root cause of errors. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a helpful step in establishing a just culture locally?

options.A: Creating transparent committees to examine workflow hazards
options.B: Acknowledging resource challenges that impact clinical care
options.C: Conducting leadership training on incident review processes
options.D: Firing any nurse immediately after their first reported error

explanation: Immediate firing suppresses reporting and destroys trust, which runs directly counter to the principles of a just culture. [learn more](GST319_U6_T5#GST319_U6_T5_h7)
